wstep: This card describes jerky made from thin strips of turkey breast, heated to 165 °F (about 74 °C) before drying and dried at 140 °F (60 °C).

ostrzezenia.tekst: According to PNW 632, poultry jerky is done and safe only when the meat has been heated to 165 °F (about 74 °C) before or immediately after drying; check the strips with a thermometer, because a dehydrator alone does not ensure this.

akapity: According to PNW 632, the best poultry cuts for jerky are breast, thigh and leg; this card covers turkey breast.
NCHFP generally does not recommend raw poultry for jerky because of the texture and flavour of the finished product.
Raw meat can be contaminated with disease-causing microorganisms, which easily multiply on moist, high-protein foods.
Keep the meat refrigerated at 40 °F (about 4 °C) or below, and use raw poultry within 2 days or freeze it.
Remove the skin and fat before drying.
Cut the meat into strips no thicker than 1/4 inch (about 6 mm).
This card does not cover jerky made from ground meat: disease-causing microorganisms are more difficult to eliminate in it than in whole-muscle strips.
Marinate the meat in the refrigerator; do not save and re-use the marinade.
Heat the turkey strips to 165 °F (about 74 °C) before drying.
A dehydrator alone does not kill microorganisms, it only inactivates them; most dehydrator instructions lack the heating step.
One way is to bring the strips and marinade to a boil and boil for 5 minutes, then drain the strips.
Another way, according to Penn State, is to bake the strips on racks in a 325 °F (163 °C) oven.
Either way, check several strips with a metal stem-type thermometer; strips thicker than 1/4 inch may need a longer boil in the marinade.
If any strip has not reached 165 °F (about 74 °C), keep heating and measure again; do not dry strips that have not reached this temperature.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): this card heats turkey only before drying, when each strip can be checked with a thermometer; it gives no oven time for heating after drying.
Dry the strips in a dehydrator or oven preheated to 140 °F (60 °C).
Do not dry meat outdoors: dry it under the controlled conditions of an oven or dehydrator.
Do not use trays or screens made of galvanized mesh; also avoid copper and aluminium mesh.
Dry the jerky until a test piece cracks but does not break when bent; strips heated in marinade dry faster than unheated ones, so begin checking them after 3 hours.
After drying, pat off beads of oil with absorbent towels, cool the jerky and package it in glass jars or heavy plastic food storage bags.
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items.
NCHFP calls vacuum packaging a good option, but it is not a preservation method by itself: removing oxygen increases the risk of botulism, and a product that needs refrigeration still needs it.
Keep properly dried jerky in a sealed container at room temperature for no more than two weeks (NCHFP); longer in the refrigerator or freezer.
Check the dried food often (glass shows condensation); if it has taken up moisture but is not spoiled, use it at once or dry it again and repack it.
Throw away mouldy jerky; also throw away any that smells off.
